# The discipline

> **Question:** what makes physical AI an engineering discipline of its own, and
> not machine learning with a motor attached?

Set a small robot on a child's desk and ask it to look at her when she speaks. To
do that one ordinary thing, it has to pick her voice out of the noise of its own
fan, decide which direction the sound came from, and turn its head before she
finishes her sentence, all without knocking over the glass of water beside it.
Notice what is not on that list: the quality of any neural network. The hard
parts are that the world would not wait, that a wrong move spills the water, and
that it had to act on a partial, noisy read of a room it cannot fully see. Those
are not model problems. They are the problems of a system coupled to the world.

## Coupling is the dividing line

::: {.column-margin}
Open loop: sense, infer, done. Closed loop: the act changes the next thing you
sense, so you live with it.
:::

A physical AI system runs in a closed loop. It senses, it decides, it acts, and
the action changes the very world it will sense next. That is the line that
separates it from its neighbors. TinyML put a model on a device and ran it:
sense, infer, perhaps actuate once, an open loop around a fixed model. A cloud
assistant answers a question and forgets both the question and the answer. A
physical AI system does neither. It lives in the consequences of its own outputs,
in real time, under the limits of a body, usually in a space that belongs to a
person. The model inside is one part. The coupling is the whole subject.

## The governing reality

Every engineering discipline answers to a reality it cannot argue with. For
machine learning systems that reality is physical law: memory bandwidth,
arithmetic intensity, the energy it takes to move a bit. For physical AI the
reality is the coupling itself, and it imposes four facts that no amount of model
quality removes.

The world does not pause. A late answer is not a slower answer; in a loop it is
the wrong answer, applied to a world that has already moved on.

Actions have consequences. A misclassification in the cloud is a wrong label. A
misclassification in a body moves something, or someone.

Sensing is partial and noisy. The system acts on a sliver of the world, read
through imperfect instruments. The map is never the territory, and the loop runs
on the map.

The device is bounded, and it lives in someone's space. Compute, power, heat,
and size are all capped, and the room it sits in is private.

## Properties before parts

From those four facts fall the elements of the discipline: the cross-cutting
properties every physical AI system must satisfy, whichever part of it you are
building. Timeliness, reliability, safety, memory and state, energy, privacy,
robustness, adaptivity, observability. [The elements](the-elements.qmd) lists
them and says how each one is measured.

The reason to name them before the components is that they are not a stage at the
end of the work. They are present wherever the coupling is present, which is
everywhere. Perception happens inside a budget of timeliness, energy, and
robustness. A decision is made inside a budget of timeliness, cost, and
observability. An action is taken inside a budget of safety and reliability. The
book therefore has two axes: the components a system is made of, and the
properties it must satisfy. The chapters walk the components; the properties run
through all of them.

## The recurring decision: placement

There is one decision the discipline makes again and again. For each capability
the system needs, where should it run? Which loop does it belong in: the reflex
loop that answers in milliseconds, the deliberation loop that takes a second to
think, or the slow learning loop that improves the system over days? And which
box should hold it: the device in the room, a server on the same network, or the
cloud? Every such choice spends some properties to buy others. Running a
capability as a reflex on the device buys timeliness and privacy and spends raw
capability. Sending it to the cloud buys capability and spends timeliness and
privacy. No placement wins on every axis. There is only the placement that is
right for this capability, under this budget, made by an engineer who can say
why, with numbers.

::: {.callout-placement}

Take the look-at-her-when-she-speaks task. Sound-source localization has to
answer in well under the length of a spoken sentence, and it runs on audio that
never leaves the room, so it belongs in the reflex loop, on the device:
timeliness and privacy are the binding properties, and the raw capability a
cloud model would add is not worth the round trip. Naming a phrase she taught
it, by contrast, can wait a beat and may borrow a larger model on the local
server. Same child, same robot, two placements, each defended by which property
binds.

:::

Learning to make and defend those choices is the skill this book teaches. What
follows is a tour of the components, read through the properties, returning each
time to the same question: where does this belong, and what did the choice cost?

::: {.callout-build title="Time the loop"}

On the kit, log a timestamp when a sound arrives and another when the head
finishes turning toward it. The gap is the loop's latency, measured rather than
assumed. Halve the sensing window and watch what the number does to the turn:
that trade, felt once, is the timeliness property made concrete.

:::

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: open with the look-at-her-when-she-speaks task and have students list
  what is hard about it before any model is mentioned. The list is the discipline.
- **Open question**: does this chapter come before or after a first hands-on
  loop? The argument for after is that students believe the properties once they
  have felt one fight them.
- **Watch**: keep the four facts concrete. The moment they harden into "constraints
  exist," the chapter has lost the reader.

:::
